title.rendered: Prophesy to the Dry Bones — The Ezekiel Pattern | How to Declare Like Jesus Did, Day 2

excerpt.rendered: God does not ask Ezekiel to pray over the bones — He tells him to prophesy to them. Day 2 teaches the sacred pattern of speaking directly to dead situations.

content.rendered:
God did not ask Ezekiel to pray over the bones. He told him to speak to them. Some situations in your life will never move until you stop talking about them and start talking to them.

The Gospel For Today | Monday, October 19, 2026 | How to Declare Like Jesus Did, Day 2

Today’s Scripture

“Again He said to me, ‘Prophesy to these bones, and say to them, “O dry bones, hear the word of the Lord!”’… So I prophesied as He commanded me, and breath came into them, and they lived, and stood upon their feet, an exceedingly great army.”
— Ezekiel 37:4, 10 (NKJV)

Today’s Message

Yesterday we laid the foundation: what God said, you say. Today we meet one of the Bible’s most arresting pictures of declaration — Ezekiel in the middle of a valley full of very dry bones. The NKJV says, “Prophesy to these bones.” The AMPC amplifies the Lord’s question that comes first: “Son of man, can these bones live?” And the TPT rendering of the moment of resurrection is startling — “as I prophesied, breath entered them… and they lived and stood up on their feet, an immense army of them.”

Notice what God did not do. He did not say, “Ezekiel, pray for these bones.” He said, “Prophesy to them.” There is a time to pray about a situation, and there is a time to speak to it. From Lagos, where a widow is standing over the bones of her finances, to London, where a young man is staring at the bones of a career dream, to Manila, where a church is grieving the bones of a vision that has not moved in years, to Nairobi and São Paulo, where a generation is tired of asking and ready to speak — the Ezekiel pattern is still God’s answer: open your mouth and say what He told you to say.

Jesus walked in this exact pattern. He spoke to the fig tree, to the wind, to demons, to fevers, and to Lazarus in the tomb. Every one of those addressees was “very dry.” Every one responded. The lesson is sobering and freeing at once: God often releases life not when we pray harder, but when we prophesy. “Can these bones live?” is not a theology question. It is an invitation. Your answer is not a wish; your answer is a word.

And notice the three stages: first the bones rattle and come together, then sinew and flesh cover them, and only then does the breath come. Declaration is a process. Do not panic between the rattle and the breath. If anything is stirring at all in the thing you have spoken to — if it looks less dead than it did a week ago — you are not failing. You are halfway through Ezekiel 37. Keep prophesying.

The Pattern of Declaration

Acknowledge. God Himself asked, “Can these bones live?” — which means He has already decided they can. Nothing in your life is beyond resurrection. The valley of dry bones is a resurrection story, not a funeral.

Personalise. Name the bones. “These bones” in your life might be a marriage, a dream, a body, a business, a child who has walked away. Do not generalise. Prophecy sharpens when it is specific.

Proclaim. Speak to the bones, not just about them. “O dry bones, hear the word of the Lord…” is the posture of a prophet, not a complainer. The breath comes after the word.

Declaration

I declare and acknowledge that nothing in my life is beyond the breath of God. The dry places hear me, because I speak the word of the Lord over them. I prophesy life to every dry bone — to my dreams that look dead, to my strength that feels spent, to the family lines that look broken, to the finances that look buried, to the ministries that have stalled. I say, “Live!” Rattle, come together, be covered, and stand up — an exceedingly great army. The breath of God enters where my words agree with His word. I will not grow weary between the rattle and the breath. I will keep prophesying until I see what God sees. In Jesus’ name. Amen.
